title: Words You Can Make From Tiles

concept.title: Every node of the search is a different word
body: You have letter tiles, some of them equal. Count the different non-empty words you can make using some or all of the tiles, each tile at most once. As with the arrangements of a word with repeats, the search chooses a **letter** (not a tile), with `count[c]` copies of every letter available: then each different word is reached by exactly one path.

Here there is no list of the word at all: the word is the **path** from the root of the search to the current call, and the call counts itself with the `1 +`. When a search only has to count, it needs no list to remember what was chosen; the counts of the unused letters are the whole state.

statement: You have `n` tiles, each with a lowercase letter; letters can repeat. Count the different non-empty words that can be made with some or all of the tiles (each tile used at most once). Words are compared as strings.
inputFormat: The only line has the letters of the tiles as one word.
outputFormat: Print the number of different words.

examples.note: The words are a, b, aa, ab, ba, aab, aba and baa: eight in total.

hints: Keep a count of the unused tiles of every letter.
Choose a letter, not a tile: equal tiles give the same word.
Every call stands for one word; add 1 and the number of longer words it can continue to.

explanation: The state is the count of unused tiles per letter. Each call tries one letter at a time; the word reached is counted once (`1 +`) and the calls below count its longer continuations.
solution.complexity: Time O(number of words * 26), at most about 10^5 words; space O(n).
